prize_parts.citation: for a body of work that remakes the boundaries between lyric, essay, narrative and visual form in dialogue with antiquity, joining formal daring to elegiac force

statement.case_for: My opening ranking stands after reconsideration. Carson's voice is distinctive at the level of the line and of the book. Autobiography of Red recasts the Geryon myth as a verse novel in which erudition, desire and comedy coexist. Nox turns elegy for a brother into an archival, material object whose form is part of its grief. Both works show formal risk joined to emotional force. This is a rare combination, and the intellectual depth comes from sustained engagement with Greek lyric and tragedy, not from decoration. The achievement has lasted across several decades, and the hybrid practice has influenced contemporary writing in English. Measured against the common criteria of voice, formal and linguistic achievement, sustained quality, depth and significance across the body of work, I find the case strongest here. It is not strongest because of the work's reception. It is strongest because the invention is of language and form, and not only of subject. I rely on general public knowledge of the main volumes and have not independently verified texts.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the oeuvre is a series of brilliant, form-driven experiments, and some of its effects depend on scholarly apparatus, book design and knowledge of the classics. These may be less stable and less widely available than sustained achievement in language. Part of the corpus is translation or adaptation of ancient texts, and some later pieces are occasional or performative. The committee must decide whether the central core is durable enough, and whether the significance extends beyond English-language and academic readerships to the idealistic direction of Nobel's will.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Carson fifth. She grants the very high intellectual depth and real formal invention, but notes that the scope is complicated by translation, scholarship and hybrid formats. She asks whether the oeuvre has a central, durable core or a series of brilliant experiments. She places Cărtărescu first for the singularity of voice and the scale of construction.
responses.response: I take the scope question seriously and agree it is the right test. My answer is that the durable core is the original work: the verse novel, the lyric and essay hybrids, and the elegy in Nox. The translations and classical adaptations are context and should not carry the citation. A well-drafted citation can say so explicitly, and the proposed wording rests on the hybrid forms and not on the translations. I also accept Mattson's point that Cărtărescu's architecture is a real and sustained achievement. Where I differ is that, on the common criteria, I weigh Carson's line-level control and formal economy more heavily than scale. I remain unsure that the visual and material formats can be judged by text alone, as Mattson also notes.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Can Xue first for an unmistakable anti-realist voice sustained over decades. He ranks Carson second, but questions whether her experiments rest on scholarly and book-design effects that are less stable than sustained achievement in language. He also notes that translation and adaptation complicate what counts as her own oeuvre.
responses.response: I partly agree. Some of Nox's force is bound up with its physical form, and I would not rest a citation on that alone. But Autobiography of Red works as a text. Its language, verse-novel form and handling of myth carry the achievement without reliance on design, and the lyric and essay work shows the same control in unadorned print. On Can Xue, I share Olsson's respect for a voice that is hers and that has been consistent for decades, and I ranked her third. My hesitation is about corpus and translation: only part of a large output is available, and the effects depend on syntax and rhythm that I cannot judge. I also find the question of whether consistency means depth or limited range harder to settle for her than for Carson.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Cărtărescu first for distinctiveness of voice, imaginative ambition and a sustained project across the Orbitor trilogy and Solenoid. He ranks Carson second and describes her line-level quality as consistently strong. He notes that her corpus is relatively compact and varied in form, which makes uniform depth harder to assess than for a large novelistic oeuvre.
responses.response: The point about uniform depth is fair. A varied oeuvre invites the question of whether quality holds across all of it, and I cannot confirm that for every volume. I would answer that depth in Carson's case is a matter of recurrent preoccupations (loss, desire, the translation of ancient material into present feeling) approached through changing forms, and not of volume. I take Sem-Sandberg's case for Cărtărescu seriously, and he is my first alternative. The length and recurring motifs of the late novels are the part that gives me pause, and Sem-Sandberg himself flags that readers may divide on whether the scale sustains itself. Judging the prose in Romanian through translation is a limit I share.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Carson first and argues that the citation should cover the hybrid oeuvre and not only the best-known verse novel. She raises the uncertainty of the work's breadth beyond English-language and academic readership, and of translation coverage of recent work.
responses.response: I agree that the citation should name the whole of the work and not a single title, and my proposed wording does so. Carlberg's reservation about significance beyond an academic readership is the one I find hardest to dismiss. I think the answer lies in the emotional directness of Nox and of the lyric, which does not require specialist knowledge. I cannot confirm that claim from reading reception, so I hold it as a judgment and not an established fact.

uncertainties: My assessment of Carson rests on general public knowledge of the main volumes and not on a full reading of the corpus, including later and occasional work.
It is unresolved how much of the achievement depends on book design, layout and classical knowledge that may not survive in other editions or in translation.
It is unresolved how the translations and adaptations of ancient texts should count within the oeuvre cited, and the citation scope needs careful wording.

Translation quality and coverage are uncertain for every shortlisted writer, especially for Cărtărescu, Can Xue and Tawada, whose effects depend on syntax, rhythm and wordplay in the source languages.

The depth of the corpus is hard to compare across candidates of different size and form, such as Carson, Michon, Wright and Cărtărescu, and the weighting of compression against range is a matter of judgment.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. The profile documents no connection to any shortlisted writer. It records only collegial connections to committee members, and I treat my own literary practice as context, not evidence for any candidate.
